newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire government ready to carry on dialogue.
newsitem.headline: Zaire government ready to carry on dialogue.

text.p: The government of President Mobutu Sese Seko said on Wednesday it was ready to continue the search for a peaceful solution to Zaire's civil war, despite the abrupt cancellation of the latest round of peace talks.

Government spokesman Kin-Kiey Mulumba said Mobutu had gone in good faith to the talks, scheduled to be held aboard a South African warship in neighbouring Congo, but rebel leader Laurent Kabila had failed to turn up.

"We do not think that the dialogue has broken down," he told reporters in Kinshasa. He said the government remained committed to "national pacification and reconciliation" and did not believe in a military solution.
"But if the logic of war must prevail, the government will act accordingly."
"The government supports and encourages every initiative undertaken in the logic of the talks in Pretoria, a logic pursued in Pointe Noire and Libreville recently," Mulumba said.
Representatives of Zaire's warring camps first met for peace talks in Pretoria in March, under South African and United Nations auspices.

Mobutu and Kabila met aboard the South African warship off Pointe Noire earlier this month and in Libreville, Gabon, a week ago, Mobutu signalled his readiness in principle to end his 32-year presidency. -- Kabila's key demand.
Mulumba said the government did not believe any durable solution could be found outside the peace process and was therefore "most attentive to everything that is happening in Pointe Noire".

Asked if he believed a second Mobutu-Kabila encounter was still possible, he replied: "I think that those who organised this summit, as you call it, will do all they can to ensure the meeting takes place."
He said the government would meet on Wednesday evening to discuss the latest turn in the fragile peace process.
The ailing Mobutu, ill with prostate cancer, spent most of Wednesday waiting for Kabila at Pointe Noire on the Atlantic coast of Congo.
Asked when he would return to Kinshasa, the spokesman said probably "not tonight" but later added "in the next hours".

Contrary to what he called rebel propaganda, the war front had stabilised some 200 km (120 miles) east of the capital and government troops were fighting with "courage and determination", Mulumba said.

The five million people of Kinshasa began their second night under military curfew at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) and troops had orders to shoot any looters. Mulumba said there was no rebel threat to Kinshasa international airport. "The city is calm," he added.

"The people of Zaire and the foreign population must accept that the country is at war, that we are in an exceptional situation and that they must accept certain privations. The curfew is not directed against (them)," he said.
Mulumba said one soldier had been killed while trying to arrest "uncontrolled elements" near the airport, but otherwise the curfew had successfully made a drastic reduction in crime.

He said the government condemned a "criminal explosion" which killed six people aboard a regular ferry crossing from the Congolese capital, Brazzaville, on Tuesday, caused by what he called a "home-made bomb".
